where W(d)∈ℝh×nW^{(d)}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times n} and 𝒇(d)∈ℝ1×n\bm{f}^{(d)}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times n} are the output weights and biases. Hidden dimension weights and biases are described above (see Eq. 60).

Appendix D Interpolation Training, Variational Optimization and Testing

In this work, we will use the NNs in two ways. The first way is called the interpolation. We train NNs on nn-RDMs computed on small L1×L2L_{1}\times L_{2} lattices to predict nn-RDMs on larger systems. This task is an interpolation, as the larger-size 𝒌\bm{k} mesh is a denser version of the smaller-size mesh. We note that in our training and predictions, the smaller meshes do not need to be subsets of the larger meshes. The second way is to use NN as variational ansatze, which will be optimized according to the chosen loss functions. The ansatze is usually directly optimized for large sizes.

In both interpolation training and variational optimization, we need to define the loss functions, and we will need to test them based on certain criteria. In this section, we will discuss the loss functions and test criteria that we may adopt. We will also provide a way to benchmark the efficiency of the model.

D.1 Loss Functions for Training and Optimization

In this part, we will discuss all the loss functions. For each loss function, we will specify the form of NN it is used for. Even if we stick to one way of using NN, we may not adopt all loss functions in all scenarios and the specific ways of using the same loss function may vary, which will be specified in App. E and App. F.

We begin with 4 loss functions that we only used for the interpolation training. First, a fundamental loss for interpolation training is the mean square error defined on our true tensor TtrueT_{\text{true}} (RDMs on small sizes) and our predicted tensor TT as

ℒm​s​e=1Card⁡(Ttrue)​∑i=1Card⁡(Ttrue)|Ti−Ttrue,i|2\mathcal{L}_{mse}={\frac{1}{\operatorname{Card}(T_{\text{true}})}\sum_{i=1}^{\operatorname{Card}(T_{\text{true}})}\left|T_{i}-T_{\text{true},i}\right|^{2}} (71)

where Card⁡(Ttrue)\operatorname{Card}(T_{\text{true}}) is the number of complex elements of TtrueT_{\text{true}}, ii labels the iith element, and |⋅||\cdot| is the modulus. This loss forces the NN output to be similar to the true data on the small meshes, providing information to interpolate from. When training on multiple meshes, the total reconstruction loss is the sum of Eq. 71 evaluated on each training tensor prediction pair (TtruesT_{\text{true}}^{s}, TsT^{s}), normalized by the mean squared magnitude of that tensor,

ℒrecon=∑sℒmse​(Ttrues,Ts)1Card⁡(Ts)​∑i|Ttrue,is|2,\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}=\sum_{s}\frac{\mathcal{L}_{\text{mse}}(T_{\text{true}}^{s},T_{s})}{\frac{1}{\operatorname{Card}(T_{s})}\sum_{i}|T_{\text{true},i}^{s}|^{2}}, (72)

so that tensors of different magnitudes contribute equally to the total loss. To be consistent, we will also use Eq. 72 even if there is only one training mesh.

Second, we define a downsampling loss for the interpolation training. For this loss, we use a bilinear interpolation to transform the predicted tensor TT on a larger 𝒌\bm{k} mesh to the smaller 𝒌\bm{k} mesh on which we have the ground truth. We call this new tensor Td​o​w​n​s​a​m​p​l​e​dT_{downsampled}. We then use Eq. 71 to find

ℒd​o​w​n​s​a​m​p​l​e=ℒm​s​e​(Ttrue,Td​o​w​n​s​a​m​p​l​e​d).\mathcal{L}_{downsample}=\mathcal{L}_{mse}(T_{\text{true}},T_{downsampled}). (73)

This is a loss to test the interpolation power.

Third, we define a symmetry loss to encourage systems to satisfy underlying symmetries (i.e., rotational symmetry) in the interpolation training. For this loss, we apply a transformation to our predicted tensor TT and calculate the MSE between the transformed tensor T′T^{\prime} and its non-transformed counterpart, giving

ℒs​y​m=ℒm​s​e​(T,T′).\mathcal{L}_{sym}=\mathcal{L}_{mse}(T,T^{\prime}). (74)

The loss will be zero if the two tensors are identical, that is when they satisfy the symmetry. This is a dimension-agnostic loss—it can be applied to any sizes mesh without knowing the ground truth.

Fourth for the interpolation training, we define a normalization loss when we wish to encourage an output to have a specific magnitude. For a scalar ss, this loss is defined as

ℒn​o​r​m=(‖T‖−s)2\mathcal{L}_{norm}=(||{T}||-s)^{2} (75)

where ||⋅||||\cdot|| represents the Frobenius norm of the tensor TT, i.e.,

‖T‖=∑i|Ti|2.\left\|T\right\|=\sqrt{\sum_{i}\left|T_{i}\right|^{2}}\ . (76)

This is a dimension-agnostic loss.

We note that for the Richardson model in App. E, we only use the above 4 losses as we will only study the pair-pair correlation function with interpolation. For the study of FCI App. F, we will not use point-group symmetry loss, downsampling loss and norm losses, but we will explicitly incorporate fermionic antisymmetry and Hermiticity. We will use the following additional losses, as we will deal with the full 2-RDM.

Regarding the NN for the full 2-RDM, we will let the NN to predict D2\prescript{2}{}{D}, and then predict Q2\prescript{2}{}{Q} and G2\prescript{2}{}{G} using the relation in Eq. 28 and Eq. 29. In particular, we will enforce the Hermiticity, PSD and antisymmetry of DD, as detailed in App. F. Then, Eq. 28 and Eq. 29 guarantee the Hermiticity of Q2\prescript{2}{}{Q} and G2\prescript{2}{}{G} and antisymmetry Q2\prescript{2}{}{Q}, but they cannot guarantee the PSD of Q2\prescript{2}{}{Q} and G2\prescript{2}{}{G}. Then, we introduce the violation of PSD Q2\prescript{2}{}{Q} and G2\prescript{2}{}{G} as a loss:

ℒP​S​DQ/G=1A​∑α=1AReLU⁡(−λαQ/G)2\mathcal{L}_{PSD_{Q/G}}=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{A}\operatorname{ReLU}\left(-\lambda_{\alpha}^{Q/G}\right)^{2} (77)

where λαQ/G\lambda^{Q/G}_{\alpha} is the α\alphath eigenvalue of Q2\prescript{2}{}{Q} or G2\prescript{2}{}{G}. As these tensors must be PSD, this pushes the prediction to be more physical, and this is a dimension-agnostic loss. This loss is used in both the interpolation training and the variational optimization.

When predicting the full 2-RDM, one can immediately predict the many-body energy EpredE_{\text{pred}}, as we only consider two-body interaction in this work. Then, we may include the energy in the loss function. For the interpolation training, we know the ground-state energy EE​DE_{ED} at small sizes, and thus we can define a loss as the distance between this energy and our predicted energy EpredE_{\text{pred}} as

ℒEd​i​s​t=(EE​D−Epred)2.\mathcal{L}_{E_{dist}}=(E_{ED}-E_{\text{pred}})^{2}. (78)

For the variational optimization on large sizes, we do not know the ground-state energy in general, and thus we directly treat the predicted EpredE_{\text{pred}} as the loss to minimize:

ℒEm​i​n=Epred.\mathcal{L}_{E_{min}}=E_{\text{pred}}\ . (79)

D.2 Testing Criteria

To evaluate the effectiveness of the architectures, two different quantities were used to benchmark the accuracy prediction. We use (i) R-value accuracy and (ii) normalized overlap, as scores defining the NN accuracy at predicting the large-size nn-RDM. For the NNs that predict the complete 2-RDMs, the PSD of predicted Q2\prescript{2}{}{Q} and G2\prescript{2}{}{G} in Eq. 77 and the many-body energy are also quantities that can benchmark the accuracy, which we will not repeat here. In the following, we discuss the R-value accuracy and normalized overlap.

D.2.1 R-value Accuracy

The R-value accuracy is previously defined [122]. We define a matrix TtrueT_{\text{true}} as our true data, and TT as our predicted data. We then have a mean square error (MSE) as defined in Eq. 71. With the mean square error, we then define an accuracy

R=1−M​S​Emax⁡(ReTtrue,ImTtrue)−min⁡(ReTtrue,ImTtrue)R=1-\frac{\sqrt{MSE}}{\max(\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}T_{\text{true}},\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}T_{\text{true}})-\min(\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}T_{\text{true}},\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}T_{\text{true}})} (80)

where Re\mathop{\mathrm{Re}} and Im\mathop{\mathrm{Im}} refer to extracting the real and imaginary components of the tensor. This gives us

Rvalue=max⁡(0,R).R_{\text{value}}=\max(0,R). (81)

This metric equals 11 for identical matrices and approaches 00 as the reconstruction error reaches or exceeds the span of the data. Because of the normalization, the error is dimensionless and directly interpretable as a score. Additionally, unlike pure MSE this normalization allows for comparison across datasets of different magnitude.

While generally useful, this metric can be misleading for sparse data. Suppose a 100×100100\times 100 zero matrix, with 4 entries of value 11 and all other entries 00. If we then use the zero matrix as the prediction TT, we will have

R=4⋅10−4\text{R}=4\cdot 10^{-4} (82)

and

R=0.98R=0.98 (83)

giving an accuracy Rvalue=0.98R_{\text{value}}=0.98. Despite this accuracy, the model has not predicted any nonzero structure.

We note that, as the normalization depends on max⁡(ReTtrue,ImTtrue)\max(\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}T_{\text{true}},\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}T_{\text{true}}) and min⁡(ReTtrue,ImTtrue)\min(\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}T_{\text{true}},\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}T_{\text{true}}), the accuracy is sensitive to outliers. Large outliers can cause the accuracy to appear far better than reality, inflating the score. Owing to these caveats, it is beneficial to develop other tools to cross check with the R-value.

D.2.2 Normalized Overlap

To cross check with the R-value, we here adopt the normalized overlap. This overlap focuses on the relative structure of the prediction and true matrix, based on the cosine of the angle between the two matrices. Using TT as our true matrix and TT as our prediction, the normalized overlap is defined as

Roverlap=|⟨Ttrue,T⟩|max⁡(∥Ttrue∥2,∥T∥2)R_{\text{overlap}}=\frac{|\langle T_{\text{true}},T\rangle|}{\max(\lVert T_{\text{true}}\rVert^{2},\lVert T\rVert^{2})} (84)

where ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle is the complex dot product and ‖T‖=⟨T,T⟩||T||=\sqrt{\langle T,T\rangle} . The value will be between 00 and 11, with a value of 11 when the two matrices are identical and 00 occurring when they are perpendicular.

As opposed to the R-value, the normalized overlap is 00 for any 00 vector prediction. Additionally, it also has an interpretable score that remains consistent across datasets of different magnitudes, and provides an understanding of how well the NN is predicting the overall structure. RoverlapR_{\text{overlap}} therefore provides a secondary score to compare with the R-value.

D.3 Parameter Efficiency

To benchmark the NN, we use the number of parameters needed to achieve a certain accuracy as a benchmark of the efficiency, leading to the parameter-efficiency plots. We benchmark the parameter efficiency only for the interpolation tasks, evaluating both the R-value and normalized overlap as a function of trainable parameters. To generate these plots, we conduct a comprehensive sweep over the architectures and hyperparameter configurations listed in App. C. For each combination, we train the model for a fixed number of epochs, recording training loss throughout the whole training and creating model checkpoints. Upon completion of training, we predict the RDM using the checkpointed model with the lowest training loss throughout, and compute the accuracy metric.

From the set of all trained configurations, we produce a scatterplot of parameter count versus accuracy. To extract a performance frontier, we partition the parameter axis into 15 bins of equal width in log⁡p\log p space, where pp is the number of parameters. Within each bin i∈0,1,…,15i\in 0,1,\dots,15, where a higher ii denotes more parameters, we select the trial achieving the highest test R-value, giving us a set of frontier points (pi,si)(p_{i},s_{i}) where pip_{i} is the parameters of this trial and sis_{i} is the best test score, both within the bin. We then enforce monotonicity along the parameter axis by setting sj′=max⁡(sj,{si}i<j)s_{j}^{\prime}=\max(s_{j},\{s_{i}\}_{i<j}) so that sj′s_{j}^{\prime} is the best achievable performance using at most pjp_{j} parameters.

These parameter-efficiency curves allow us to determine the model capacity required to accurately reconstruct large-size mesh nn-RDMs from small-size mesh inputs. We are also able to quickly determine which NN classes are best at this form of machine learning, and compare different losses’ effect on training.

Appendix E Richardson Model Training

In this section, we train NNs to predict the pair-pair correlation function of the ground states of the Richardson model. The models are trained on small sizes and thus this is the interpolation way of using NNs. This is an exactly solvable model, allowing us to verify that our different NNs are able to interpolate in this simple case before attempting on a more complex material.

E.1 Model Setup

The Richardson model of superconductivity [196, 197, 198] has the Hamiltonian

H=∑𝒌,sε𝒌​c𝒌,s†​c𝒌,s+uL2​(∑𝒌A𝒌†)​(∑𝒌′A𝒌′).H=\sum_{\bm{k},s}\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k},s}c_{\bm{k},s}+\frac{u}{L^{2}}\left(\sum_{\bm{k}}A^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}\right)\left(\sum_{\bm{k^{\prime}}}A_{\bm{k^{\prime}}}\right). (85)

where c𝒌​s†c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}s} creates an electron at Bloch momnetum 𝒌\bm{k} and spin ss, A𝒌†=c𝒌,↑†​c−𝒌,↓†A^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}=c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k},\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k},\downarrow} is the Cooper-pair operator, u<0u<0 denotes attractive interaction, ε𝒌=t⁡(cos⁡kx+cos⁡ky)\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}=t(\cos k_{x}+\cos k_{y}), and 𝒌\bm{k} takes value from an L1×L2L_{1}\times L_{2} mesh. We particularly focus on the pair-pair correlation function

Ct​r​u​e,𝒌​𝒌′≡⟨A𝒌†​A𝒌′⟩−⟨A𝒌†⟩​⟨A𝒌′⟩.C_{true,\bm{kk}^{\prime}}\equiv\langle A^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}A_{\bm{k^{\prime}}}\rangle-\langle A^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}\rangle\langle A_{\bm{k^{\prime}}}\rangle. (86)

where ⟨…⟩\langle\dots\rangle is the average with respect to the ground state in the total-spin-zero sector. We will use C𝒌​𝒌′C_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}} as the predicted one. Due to the spinless time-reversal and inversion symmetry, we have the pair-pair correlation function of the Richardson Model C∈ℝNk×NkC\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{k}\times N_{k}}. The pair-pair correlation function is a special set of components of the 2-RDM, as ⟨A𝒌†⟩=0\langle A^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}\rangle=0 for the particle-number-conserved states considered here. The Hermiticity and PSD condition of D2\prescript{2}{}{D} then are reduced to C𝒌​𝒌′C_{\bm{kk}^{\prime}} being a symmetric PSD real matrix, and we will not consider other NN-representability constraints. Same as Ref. [122], we use a fixed electron filling of ν=N/Nk=1/6\nu=N/N_{k}=1/6.

E.2 Training Data and Preprocessing

For the Richardson Model, we train the NN on both a conventional 6×66\times 6 mesh and 4 tilted meshes each of which has 12 𝒌\bm{k} points. We then predict on an conventional 18×1818\times 18 mesh. We will provide a general discuss on both ways, and then describe the differences. Both methods train on the dominant component. Specifically, in Fig. 6 we see the ordered list of eigenvalues of the pair-pair correlation function for the training data and note that only one eigenvalue dominates. Because of this, we may express an approximation of the full pair-pair correlation function as

C=λ​v~​v~†,C=\lambda\tilde{v}\tilde{v}^{\dagger}\ , (87)

where λ\lambda is the dominant eigenvalue and v~\tilde{v} is the dominant normalized eigenvector. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this calculation, we consider primary eigenvalue-eigenvector pair of the true pair-pair correlation function on the 6×66\times 6 𝒌\bm{k} point mesh, that is the pair with the highest eigenvalue. When using this 1-eigenvalue construction as a prediction on the true data could then have a normalized overlap of 0.999970.99997 and an R-value of 0.9960.996.

In order to find an appropriate eigenvalue, we note that the trace of the physical pair-pair correlation function is always

Tr(C)=Nk12,\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}(C)=\frac{N_{k}}{12}\ , (88)

where the 1/12 comes from half the electron filling (which represents the Cooper pair filling). In the training, we fix the value of λ\lambda to be the largest eigenvalue from the training data, and in the prediction, we will scale it by

λp​r​e​d=λt​r​a​i​n​Nkp​r​e​d​i​c​t​i​o​nNkt​r​a​i​n​i​n​g.\lambda_{pred}=\lambda_{train}\frac{N_{k}^{prediction}}{N_{k}^{training}}\ . (89)

Note that Nkp​r​e​d​i​c​t​i​o​nN_{k}^{prediction} is the input for the prediction, as it is just the number of 𝒌\bm{k} points in the mesh on which the prediction is performed. So we are not using any large-size test data to train the model. On the other hand, v~\tilde{v} in Eq. 87 is what the NN will learn to predict.

To train the NN for v~\tilde{v}, we first compute the eigen decomposition of the training data, which gives the dominating eigenvector vv, which we take as ‖v‖=1\|v\|=1. After that, we preprocess the dominant eigenvector as a NN input. We first normalize the coordinates used for predicting the NN output, mapping each 𝒌\bm{k} to a point in [−1,1]2[-1,1]^{2} and applying periodic boundary conditions; this transforms the eigenvector’s shape to (L1+1)×(L2+1)(L_{1}+1)\times(L_{2}+1), and we refer to the periodic eigenvector as vwv_{w}. We then apply the element-wise standardization

vw′=vw−μσv_{w}^{\prime}=\frac{v_{w}-\mu}{\sigma} (90)

where vw′v^{\prime}_{w} is the modified vector and μ\mu and σ\sigma are the mean and standard deviation of vwv_{w}. This process is reversible, with a de-scaling given by

vw=vw′​σ+μ.v_{w}=v_{w}^{\prime}\sigma+\mu. (91)

When using the NN to predict our pair-pair correlation function we apply this descaling Eq. 91 to the NN output v~w′\tilde{v}_{w}^{\prime}, which has the same standardization as vw′v_{w}^{\prime}, using the same σ\sigma and μ\mu of the dominant training eigenvector. We then enforce the four-fold rotational symmetry and Hermiticity on this output by computing and averaging each symmetry transformation, cropping the periodic boundary to recover v~\tilde{v}, and enforcing ‖v~‖=1\|\tilde{v}\|=1 before reconstructing the pair-pair correlation function with Eq. 87.

During training, we incorporate four different losses: a small data loss, a downsampling loss, a symmetry loss, and a unit-norm loss as defined in Sec. D.1. For these losses, we consider the vector v~s\tilde{v}_{s} predicted by our NN over the small 𝒌\bm{k} and v~l\tilde{v}_{l} predicted over the large 𝒌\bm{k} mesh. For the small data loss, we use Eq. 71 to calculate the MSE between v~s\tilde{v}_{s} and vv. For the downsampling loss, we use Eq. 73, predicting the large-size tensor and downsampling to compare to the small-size tensor. For the symmetry loss, Eq. 74, we use the four-fold rotational symmetry and Hermiticity (which is simplifed to transpose due to CC being real). This loss is applied after 2020 epochs, ensuring they don’t overpower the loss of the NN. For the Norm loss defined in Eq. 75 we take s=1s=1, ensuring the vector is normalized.

Hence, the total loss is

ℒ=αsmall​ℒsmall+αinterp​ℒdownsample+αsym​ℒsym+αnorm​ℒnorm\mathcal{L}=\alpha_{\text{small}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{small}}+\alpha_{\text{interp}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{downsample}}+\alpha_{\text{sym}}\mathcal{L_{\text{sym}}}+\alpha_{\text{norm}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{norm}} (92)

where the weightings of these losses can be seen in Tab. 7.

We use the Adam optimizer [212] and train all models for 1000 epochs and use a learning rate of 10−410^{-4}.

The above method is what we use for the training on the conventional 6×66\times 6 mesh. For the training on the 4 1212-𝒌\bm{k} meshes, we note that the fact that there is only one Cooper pair for each mesh, we always choose λt​r​a​i​n​i​n​g=1\lambda_{training}=1 for all meshes.

For the dominant eigenvectors of all meshes, we combine them by merging the 4 momentum meshes into a single set of 𝒌\bm{k} points, with each point in each mesh carrying the corresponding component of the eigenvector in its original mesh. A visualization of the chosen 𝒌\bm{k} points can be seen in Fig. 7. Because the tilted mesh training consists of scattered 𝒌\bm{k} rather than a regular grid, the interpolation loss ℒi​n​t​e​r​p\mathcal{L}_{interp} and the unit-norm loss ℒn​o​r​m\mathcal{L}_{norm} are not applicable. Everything else about the training is in the same way as that on the conventional 6×66\times 6 mesh.

E.3 ML Results

In this section, we evaluate the performance of our NN architectures for training on both a 6×66\times 6 𝒌\bm{k} point mesh and on 4 tilted 12−𝒌12-\bm{k} meshes of the Richardson model’s pair-pair correlation function. The prediction is then evaluated on the 18×1818\times 18 mesh.

E.3.1 Trained on 6×66\times 6 Mesh

When trained on the 6×66\times 6 mesh, each architecture is able to reach a similar level of performance, though the number of needed parameters is different, as shown in Tab. 8. This table provides the best R-value of each architecture over our parameter sweep. We find that KAN achieves the best R-value of 0.985720.98572 and a normalized overlap of 0.970280.97028, while the TBN is the worst NN with an R-value of 0.983710.98371 and a normalized overlap of 0.970130.97013. Nevertheless, the values are close, and do not provide much information about the true differences between these models. We also examine the best prediction, in Fig. 8. This provides the true data and the prediction. The NN does a very good job of predicting the original data, only missing a perturbation along the diagonal of the original data.

We can also examine the parameter efficiency, as seen in Fig. 9. These plots show us how the NNs adapt in accuracy with the number of parameters. Both the SIREN and the FINER, which are designed for INR, outperform all models at lower parameters, with SIREN performing the best. The performance continues until around 10001000 total parameters, when the accuracy saturates and all models reach a similar level of performance.

For the KAN, we found the optimal model with 791,040791,040 parameters, a depth of 33, a hidden dimension of 256256 a grid size of 1, a base scale of 1, and a spline scale of 5. For the MLP, we found the optimal model with 33,53733,537 parameters, a depth of 33 and a hidden dimension of 128128. For the Residual MLP, we found the optimal model with 1,982,4651,982,465 parameters, a depth of 4040, and a hidden dimension of 256256. For the SIREN, we found the optimal model with 3,2973,297 parameters, a depth of 33, a hidden dimension of 3232, a ω0\omega_{0} of 6, and an ω1\omega_{1} of 55. For the FINER, we found the optimal model with 12,73712,737 parameters, a depth of 33, a hidden dimension of 6464, and both ω0\omega_{0} and ω1\omega_{1} of 11. Finally, for the TBN, we found an optimal model with 339,105 parameters, a depth of 2, a hidden dimension of 128128, no dropout, 2 heads, and 4 frequencies.

Finally, as our current data is dominated by a single eigenvalue, we evaluate the performance of just a simple Fourier representation of the data. When computing the fast Fourier Transform (FFT) on the small-size 6×66\times 6 mesh, applying a zero-padding to the frequency domain to provide the same dimension of the large-size data, and using an inverse FFT to reconstruct the data, we find an R-value of 0.983790.98379 and a normalized overlap of 0.9700560.970056. Hence, most of our results can be closely approximated by simple techniques. However, we were able to achieve scores slightly higher than this result, showing the promise of our method.

E.3.2 Trained on Tilted Meshes

When trained on tilted meshes (each of which has 12 momenta), each architecture is again able to reach a similar level of performance, as shown in Tab. 9. This table provides the best R-value of each architecture over our parameter sweep. We find that KAN achieves the best R-value of 0.954270.95427 and a normalized overlap of 0.9078050.907805, while the FINER is the worst NN with an R-value of 0.954080.95408 and a normalized overlap of 0.9075530.907553. Again, the values are extremely close, and do not provide much information about the true differences between these models. We may also examine a plot of the best prediction in Fig. 10. Here, we see a slightly less accurate prediction, as λt​r​a​i​n​i​n​g=1\lambda_{training}=1 is fixed for the tilted meshes. With a properly chosen eigenvalue, that is the actual eigenvalue found during eigendecomposition of the large-size data, we have a potential R-value as high as 0.9875200.987520. We note that, when doing any future interpolation based on training the eigendecomposition, special care must be taken in finding eigenvalues for reconstruction.

We also examine the parameter efficiency, as seen in Fig. 11. These plots show us how the architectures change with number of parameters, and we can see a leveling off around 10001000 parameters, as before. The performance of each model is analogous to those trained on the 6×66\times 6 mesh.

For the KAN, we found the optimal model with 7,680 parameters, a depth of 1, a hidden dimension of 256, a grid size of 5, a base scale of 1, and a spline scale of 5. For the MLP, we found the optimal model with 17,025 parameters, a depth of 2, and a hidden dimension of 128. For the Residual MLP, we found the optimal model with 23,10523,105 parameters, a depth of 2020, and a hidden dimension of 8. For the SIREN, we found the optimal model with 337 parameters, a depth of 1, a hidden dimension of 16, a first ω0\omega_{0} of 1212, and a hidden ω1\omega_{1} of 5. For the FINER we found the optimal model with 337 parameters, a depth of 1, a hidden dimension of 16, a first ω0\omega_{0} of 1.0, and a hidden ω1\omega_{1} of 0.10.1. Finally, for the TBN, we found the optimal model with 301,185 parameters, a depth of 6, a hidden dimension of 64, 1 head, 4 frequencies, and no dropout.

Finally, as our current data is dominated by a single eigenvalue, we evaluate the performance of just a simple Fourier representation of the data. Unlike the previous method, we must first modify the data in order for FFT upscaling to work. First, the dominant eigenvector is computed exactly from each training file’s pair-pair correlation function, then its values at the 𝒌\bm{k} points are interpolated onto a uniform 12×1212\times 12 𝒌\bm{k} point grid using cubic interpolation. Cubic interpolation fits piecewise cubic polynomials between data points and matching first derivatives, creating a smooth transition between the points. We then do the same upscaling as before, going to our 18×1818\times 18 𝒌\bm{k} point mesh with the FFT zero-padding. The pair-pair correlation function is then reconstructed using 18227​v​vT\frac{18^{2}}{27}{v}{v}^{T}. With this method, we find a normalized overlap of 0.9071130.907113 and an R-value of 0.519470.51947 providing a non-learned baseline. We note that the additional cubic interpolation step required by irregular sampling introduces an extra approximation not present in the 6×66\times 6 mesh baseline. The neural networks are able to exceed this baseline, demonstrating they provide some useful structure beyond simple Fourier methods.

Appendix F Twisted Bilayer MoTe2

In this section, we examine how different NNs are able to interpolate the 2-RDM of twisted bilayer MoTe2, and further examine their ability to be variationally minimized and predict the ground-state 2-RDMs and energy of the system.

F.1 Model Formulation

We first start with a brief review of the K-valley model for ttMoTe2 [128] that we use in this work. The non-interacting part of the model has a general form

HK,0h=−∑Mx,My∈ℕ∑l,l′=t,b∫d2r(iMx+My∂xMx∂yMyc~K,l,𝒓†)tl​l′Mx​My(𝒓)c~K,l′,𝒓H_{\text{K},0}^{h}=-\sum_{M_{x},M_{y}\in\mathbb{N}}\sum_{l,l^{\prime}=t,b}\int d^{2}r\left(\mathrm{i}^{M_{x}+M_{y}}\partial_{x}^{M_{x}}\partial_{y}^{M_{y}}\widetilde{c}^{\dagger}_{\text{K},l,\bm{r}}\right)t^{M_{x}M_{y}}_{ll^{\prime}}(\bm{r})\widetilde{c}_{\text{K},l^{\prime},\bm{r}} (93)

where c~K,l,𝒓†\widetilde{c}_{\text{K},l,\bm{r}}^{\dagger} is the creation operator for a hole in the K valley in the llth layer at position 𝒓\bm{r}, and ℕ\mathbb{N} denotes the set of non-negative integers. The detailed form of tl​l′Mx​Myt^{M_{x}M_{y}}_{ll^{\prime}} is Ref. [165], and we use the parameter values for twist angle 3.89∘3.89^{\circ}. Those parameters are derived from density functional theory (DFT) calculations without any continuous parameter fitting.

For the interaction, we adopt

HK,i​n​th=12​∑l​l′∫d2​r​d2​r′​V​(𝒓−𝒓′)​c~K,l,𝒓†​c~K,l′,𝒓′†​c~K,l′,𝒓′​c~K,l,𝒓,H_{\text{K},int}^{h}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ll^{\prime}}\int d^{2}rd^{2}r^{\prime}V(\bm{r}-\bm{r}^{\prime})\widetilde{c}^{\dagger}_{\text{K},l,\bm{r}}\widetilde{c}^{\dagger}_{\text{K},l^{\prime},\bm{r}^{\prime}}\widetilde{c}_{\text{K},l^{\prime},\bm{r}^{\prime}}\widetilde{c}_{\text{K},l,\bm{r}}\ , (94)

which is the double-gated screened Coulomb potential V⁡(𝒓)V(\bm{r}) with gate distance ξ\xi:

V⁡(𝒓)=∫ℝ2d2​p(2​π)2​V​(𝒑)​ei​𝒑⋅𝒓​ with ​V​(𝒑)=e24​ϵr​ϵ0​tanh⁡(ξ​|𝒑|/2)|𝒑|/2,V(\bm{r})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\frac{d^{2}p}{(2\pi)^{2}}V(\bm{p})e^{\mathrm{i}\bm{p}\cdot\bm{r}}\text{ with }V(\bm{p})=\frac{e^{2}}{4\epsilon_{r}\epsilon_{0}}\frac{\tanh(\xi|\bm{p}|/2)}{|\bm{p}|/2}\ , (95)

where ϵ0\epsilon_{0} is the vacuum permittivity, and ϵr\epsilon_{r} is the relative dielectric constant.

We then diagonalize the noninteracting part of the Hamiltonian in the momentum space, project continuum many-body Hamiltonian to the subspace of the lowest hole band, and obtain

H=∑𝒌c𝒌†​c𝒌​ϵ𝒌+∑𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒V⁡(𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒)​c−𝒌+𝒒†​c𝒌†​c𝒌′​c−𝒌′+𝒒,\displaystyle\begin{split}H&=\sum_{\bm{k}}c_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k}}\epsilon_{\bm{k}}+\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}V(\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q})c_{-\bm{k}+\bm{q}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}c_{-\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{q}}\ ,\end{split} (96)

where

c𝒌†=∑𝑸c~K,𝒌,𝑸†​U𝑸​(𝒌)c_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}=\sum_{\bm{Q}}\widetilde{c}_{\text{K},\bm{k},\bm{Q}}^{\dagger}U_{\bm{Q}}(\bm{k}) (97)

with U⁡(𝒌)U(\bm{k}) the eigenvector of the lowest hole band with eigenvalue ϵ𝒌\epsilon_{\bm{k}} at the Bloch momentum 𝒌\bm{k} and c~K,𝒌,𝑸†\widetilde{c}_{\text{K},\bm{k},\bm{Q}}^{\dagger} the Fourier transformation of c~K,l,𝒓†\widetilde{c}^{\dagger}_{\text{K},l,\bm{r}}. We choose the shortest 60 𝑸\bm{Q} vectors for the projection, ξ=20​nm\xi=20\,\mathrm{nm} and ϵr=10\epsilon_{r}=10. All the U⁡(𝒌)U(\bm{k}) on all the meshes are selected from the U⁡(𝒌)U(\bm{k}) on a conventional 60×6060\times 60 mesh in the parallel transport gauge to make sure the continuity inside the 1BZ, though the continuity cannot be across the 1BZboundary due to the obstruction of the Chern number. (See details in Ref. [165].)

F.2 Parametrization of RDMs

In the case of the projected ttMoTe22, the physical 2-RDMs reads

Dtrue𝒌1​𝒌2​𝒌3​𝒌42=⟨c𝒌1†​c𝒌2†​c𝒌3​c𝒌4⟩Qtrue𝒌1​𝒌2​𝒌3​𝒌42=⟨c𝒌1​c𝒌2​c𝒌3†​c𝒌4†⟩Gtrue𝒌1​𝒌2​𝒌3​𝒌42=⟨c𝒌1†​c𝒌2​c𝒌3†​c𝒌4⟩.\displaystyle\begin{split}&\prescript{2}{}{D}_{\bm{k}_{1}\bm{k}_{2}\bm{k}_{3}\bm{k}_{4}}^{\rm true}=\left\langle c_{\bm{k}_{1}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k}_{2}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k}_{3}}c_{\bm{k}_{4}}\right\rangle\\ &\prescript{2}{}{Q}_{\bm{k}_{1}\bm{k}_{2}\bm{k}_{3}\bm{k}_{4}}^{\rm true}=\left\langle c_{\bm{k}_{1}}c_{\bm{k}_{2}}c_{\bm{k}_{3}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k}_{4}}^{\dagger}\right\rangle\\ &\prescript{2}{}{G}_{\bm{k}_{1}\bm{k}_{2}\bm{k}_{3}\bm{k}_{4}}^{\rm true}=\left\langle c_{\bm{k}_{1}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k}_{2}}c_{\bm{k}_{3}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k}_{4}}\right\rangle\ .\end{split} (98)

We always consider the 2-RDMs that are generated by one ground state with a definite many-body momentum. Therefore, the physical and the predicted 2-RDMs must respect the momentum conservation:

D𝒌1​𝒌2​𝒌3​𝒌42=0​ if ​𝒌1+𝒌2≠𝒌3+𝒌4​mod​𝑮MQ𝒌1​𝒌2​𝒌3​𝒌42=0​ if ​𝒌1+𝒌2≠𝒌3+𝒌4​mod​𝑮MG𝒌1​𝒌2​𝒌3​𝒌42=0​ if ​𝒌1+𝒌3=𝒌2+𝒌4​mod​𝑮M,\displaystyle\begin{split}&\prescript{2}{}{D}_{\bm{k}_{1}\bm{k}_{2}\bm{k}_{3}\bm{k}_{4}}=0\text{ if }\bm{k}_{1}+\bm{k}_{2}\neq\bm{k}_{3}+\bm{k}_{4}\ \mathrm{mod}\ \bm{G}_{M}\\ &\prescript{2}{}{Q}_{\bm{k}_{1}\bm{k}_{2}\bm{k}_{3}\bm{k}_{4}}=0\text{ if }\bm{k}_{1}+\bm{k}_{2}\neq\bm{k}_{3}+\bm{k}_{4}\ \mathrm{mod}\ \bm{G}_{M}\\ &\prescript{2}{}{G}_{\bm{k}_{1}\bm{k}_{2}\bm{k}_{3}\bm{k}_{4}}=0\text{ if }\bm{k}_{1}+\bm{k}_{3}=\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{k}_{4}\ \mathrm{mod}\ \bm{G}_{M}\ ,\end{split} (99)

where 𝑮M\bm{G}_{M} is the moiré reciprocal lattice vector. With this knowledge, we are able to include momentum conservation to reduce the number of parameters per model from ∼Nk4\sim N_{k}^{4} to ∼Nk3\sim N_{k}^{3}, improving the computational feasibility of the training. Explicitly, the elements that are allowed to be nonzero are simply

D~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2=D−𝒌+𝒒,𝒌,𝒌′,−𝒌′+𝒒2Q~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2=Q−𝒌+𝒒,𝒌,𝒌′,−𝒌′+𝒒2G~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2=G𝒌+𝒒,𝒌,𝒌′,𝒌′+𝒒2.\displaystyle\begin{split}&\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}=\prescript{2}{}{D}_{-\bm{k}+\bm{q},\,\bm{k},\,\bm{k}^{\prime},\,-\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{q}}\\ &\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{Q}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}=\prescript{2}{}{Q}_{-\bm{k}+\bm{q},\,\bm{k},\,\bm{k}^{\prime},\,-\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{q}}\\ &\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{G}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}=\prescript{2}{}{G}_{\bm{k}+\bm{q},\,\bm{k},\,\bm{k}^{\prime},\,\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{q}}.\end{split} (100)

Given a predicted D~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}, the corresponding many-body energy reads

Epred=1N−1​∑𝒌,𝒒ϵ𝒌​D~𝒌,𝒌,𝒒2​(x)+∑𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒V𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒​D~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2.E_{\text{pred}}=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{q}}\epsilon_{\bm{k}}\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k},\bm{q}}(x)+\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}V_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}\ . (101)

The translational invariance reduces the Hermiticity to

D~∗𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2=D~𝒌′,𝒌,𝒒2Q~∗𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2=Q~𝒌′,𝒌,𝒒2G~∗𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2=G~𝒌′,𝒌,𝒒2\displaystyle\begin{split}&\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}^{*}=\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{k},\bm{q}}\\ &\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{Q}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}^{*}=\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{Q}}_{\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{k},\bm{q}}\\ &\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{G}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}^{*}=\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{G}}_{\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{k},\bm{q}}\end{split} (102)

equivalent to D~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}} being a hermitian matrix with index 𝒌​𝒌′\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime} for each 𝒒\bm{q} (similarly for Q~2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{Q}} and G~2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{G}}), and the antisymmetry of D2\prescript{2}{}{D} and Q2\prescript{2}{}{Q} to

D~−𝒌+𝒒,𝒌′,𝒒2=D~𝒌,−𝒌′+𝒒,𝒒2=−D~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2Q~−𝒌+𝒒,𝒌′,𝒒2=Q~𝒌,−𝒌′+𝒒,𝒒2=−Q~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2.\displaystyle\begin{split}&\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{-\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}=\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},-\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{q},\bm{q}}=-\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}\\ &\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{Q}}_{-\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}=\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{Q}}_{\bm{k},-\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{q},\bm{q}}=-\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{Q}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}\ .\end{split} (103)

The particle number constraints are

∑𝒌,𝒒D~𝒌,𝒌,𝒒2=N⁡(N−1)∑𝒌,𝒒Q~𝒌,𝒌,𝒒2=(Nk−N)​(Nk−N−1)∑𝒌,𝒌′G~𝒌,𝒌′,𝟎2=N2.\displaystyle\begin{split}&\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{q}}\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k},\bm{q}}=N(N-1)\\ &\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{q}}\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{Q}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k},\bm{q}}=(N_{k}-N)(N_{k}-N-1)\\ &\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{G}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{0}}=N^{2}\ .\end{split} (104)

The PSD of D2\prescript{2}{}{D} now can be simplified as

∑𝒌1​𝒌2​𝒌3​𝒌4Y𝒌𝟏​𝒌𝟐​D𝒌𝟏​𝒌𝟐​𝒌𝟑​𝒌𝟒2​Y𝒌𝟒​𝒌𝟑⋆≥0⇔∑𝒌1​𝒌2​𝒌3​𝒌4Y𝒌𝟏​𝒌𝟐​∑𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒δ𝒌1,−𝒌+𝒒​mod​𝑮M​δ𝒌2,𝒌​D−𝒌+𝒒,𝒌,𝒌′,−𝒌′+𝒒2​δ𝒌4,−𝒌′+𝒒​mod​𝑮M​δ𝒌3,𝒌′​Y𝒌𝟒​𝒌𝟑⋆≥0⇔∑𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒Y−𝒌+𝒒,𝒌​D−𝒌+𝒒,𝒌,𝒌′,−𝒌′+𝒒2​Y−𝒌′+𝒒,𝒌′⋆≥0⇔∑𝒒∑𝒌,𝒌′y𝒒,𝒌​D−𝒌+𝒒,𝒌,𝒌′,−𝒌′+𝒒2​y𝒒,𝒌⋆≥0⇔∑𝒒∑𝒌,𝒌′y𝒒,𝒌​D~𝒌,𝒌,𝒒2​y𝒒,𝒌⋆≥0\displaystyle\begin{split}&\sum_{\bm{k}_{1}\bm{k}_{2}\bm{k}_{3}\bm{k}_{4}}Y_{\bm{k_{1}}\bm{k_{2}}}\prescript{2}{}{D}_{\bm{k_{1}}\bm{k_{2}}\bm{k_{3}}\bm{k_{4}}}Y^{\star}_{\bm{k_{4}}\bm{k_{3}}}\geq 0\\ &\Leftrightarrow\sum_{\bm{k}_{1}\bm{k}_{2}\bm{k}_{3}\bm{k}_{4}}Y_{\bm{k_{1}}\bm{k_{2}}}\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}\delta_{\bm{k}_{1},-\bm{k}+\bm{q}\mathrm{mod}\bm{G}_{M}}\delta_{\bm{k}_{2},\bm{k}}\prescript{2}{}{D}_{-\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},-\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{q}}\delta_{\bm{k}_{4},-\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{q}\mathrm{mod}\bm{G}_{M}}\delta_{\bm{k}_{3},\bm{k}^{\prime}}Y^{\star}_{\bm{k_{4}}\bm{k_{3}}}\geq 0\\ &\Leftrightarrow\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}Y_{-\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{k}}\prescript{2}{}{D}_{-\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},-\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{q}}Y^{\star}_{-\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{q},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\geq 0\\ &\Leftrightarrow\sum_{\bm{q}}\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}y_{\bm{q},\bm{k}}\prescript{2}{}{D}_{-\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},-\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{q}}y_{\bm{q},\bm{k}}^{\star}\geq 0\\ &\Leftrightarrow\sum_{\bm{q}}\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}y_{\bm{q},\bm{k}}\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k},\bm{q}}y_{\bm{q},\bm{k}}^{\star}\geq 0\end{split} (105)

for any complex y𝒒,𝒌=Y−𝒌+𝒒,𝒌y_{\bm{q},\bm{k}}=Y_{-\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{k}}. It means that the PSD of D2\prescript{2}{}{D} is equivalent to that D~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}} being a PSD matrix of index 𝒌​𝒌′\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime} for each 𝒒\bm{q}. Similarly, the PSD of Q2\prescript{2}{}{Q} equivalent to that Q~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{Q}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}} being a PSD matrix of index 𝒌​𝒌′\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime} for each 𝒒\bm{q}, and the PSD of G2\prescript{2}{}{G} equivalent to that G~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{G}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}} being a PSD matrix of index 𝒌​𝒌′\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime} for each 𝒒\bm{q}.

For our NNs, we parameterize D~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}} as

D~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2=(A𝒒​A𝒒†)𝒌,𝒌′\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}=(A_{\bm{q}}A_{\bm{q}}^{\dagger})_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}} (106)

with A𝒒A_{\bm{q}} a complex matrix of size Nk×NkN_{k}\times N_{k}. Our NN directly predicts A𝒒A_{\bm{q}}, and antisymmetrize it via

[A𝒒]𝒌,𝒑→([A𝒒]𝒌,𝒑−[A𝒒]−𝒌+𝒒,𝒑)/2\left[A_{\bm{q}}\right]_{\bm{k},\bm{p}}\rightarrow(\left[A_{\bm{q}}\right]_{\bm{k},\bm{p}}-\left[A_{\bm{q}}\right]_{-\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{p}})/2 (107)

for all 𝒌,𝒒,𝒑\bm{k},\bm{q},\bm{p}. It then predicts D~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}} via Eq. 106, and then predicts Q~2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{Q}} and G~2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{G}} via Eq. 29 and Eq. 28, respectively. Due to the Hermiticity and antisymmetry of D~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}, the AS and Hermiticity of Q~2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{Q}} and the Hermiticity of G~2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{G}} are automatically guaranteed, owing to Eqs. 29 and 28. In addition, we also guarantee the particle number constraint by normalizing the predicted D~2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}} to N⁡(N−1)N(N-1), which particle number constraints of Q~2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{Q}} and the Hermiticity of G~2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{G}}, owing to Eqs. 29 and 28. Then, the only remaining (2,2)(2,2) conditions are the PSD of Q~2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{Q}} and G~2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{G}}, which we treated as the PSD loss, as discussed in Sec. D.1.

In addition, the translational invariance can also simplify the parametrization of the 3-RDM such as

Dtrue−𝒌1′−𝒌2′+𝒒,𝒌1,𝒌2,𝒌2′,𝒌1′,−𝒌1−𝒌2+𝒒3=⟨c−𝒌1−𝒌2+𝒒†​c𝒌1†​c𝒌2†​c𝒌2′​c𝒌1′​c−𝒌1′−𝒌2′+𝒒⟩=D~true𝒌1,𝒌2,𝒌2′,𝒌1′,𝒒3Qtrue−𝒌1−𝒌2+𝒒,𝒌1,𝒌2,𝒌2′,𝒌1′,−𝒌1′−𝒌2′+𝒒3=⟨c−𝒌1−𝒌2+𝒒​c𝒌1​c𝒌2​c𝒌2′†​c𝒌1′†​c−𝒌1′−𝒌2′+𝒒†⟩=Q~true𝒌1,𝒌2,𝒌2′,𝒌1′,𝒒3.\displaystyle\begin{split}\prescript{3}{}{D}_{-\bm{k}_{1}^{\prime}-\bm{k}_{2}^{\prime}+\bm{q},\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2},\bm{k}_{2}^{\prime},\bm{k}_{1}^{\prime},-\bm{k}_{1}-\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{q}}^{\rm true}&=\left\langle c^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}_{1}-\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{q}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}_{1}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}_{2}}c_{\bm{k}_{2}^{\prime}}c_{\bm{k}_{1}^{\prime}}c_{-\bm{k}_{1}^{\prime}-\bm{k}_{2}^{\prime}+\bm{q}}\right\rangle=\prescript{3}{}{\widetilde{D}}_{\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2},\bm{k}_{2}^{\prime},\bm{k}_{1}^{\prime},\bm{q}}^{\rm true}\\ \prescript{3}{}{Q}_{-\bm{k}_{1}-\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{q},\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2},\bm{k}_{2}^{\prime},\bm{k}_{1}^{\prime},-\bm{k}_{1}^{\prime}-\bm{k}_{2}^{\prime}+\bm{q}}^{\rm true}&=\left\langle c_{-\bm{k}_{1}-\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{q}}c_{\bm{k}_{1}}c_{\bm{k}_{2}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}_{2}^{\prime}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}_{1}^{\prime}}c^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}_{1}^{\prime}-\bm{k}_{2}^{\prime}+\bm{q}}\right\rangle=\prescript{3}{}{\widetilde{Q}}_{\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2},\bm{k}_{2}^{\prime},\bm{k}_{1}^{\prime},\bm{q}}^{\rm true}\ .\end{split} (108)

F.3 Many-body quantum metric from 2-RDM

The many-body quantum metric is defined by the tracking the evolution of the many-body state under twist boundary condition [199, 200, 201, 202, 203, 204, 205]. Specifically, given |Ψ(𝒒)⟩\left|{\Psi(\bm{q})}\right> with twist-boundary condition 𝒒\bm{q}, we define

|Φ𝒒⟩=e−i𝒒⋅𝑿|Ψ(𝒒)⟩,\left|{\Phi_{\bm{q}}}\right>=e^{-\mathrm{i}\bm{q}\cdot\bm{X}}\left|{\Psi(\bm{q})}\right>\ , (109)

where 𝑿\bm{X} is the many-body position operator

𝑿=∫d2​r​∑l𝒓​c~K,l,𝒓†​c~K,l,𝒓.\bm{X}=\int d^{2}r\sum_{l}\bm{r}\widetilde{c}^{\dagger}_{\text{K},l,\bm{r}}\widetilde{c}_{\text{K},l,\bm{r}}\ . (110)

Then, the many-body quantum metric reads

gi​jmb​(𝒒)=12⟨∂qiΦ𝒒|(1−|Φ𝒒⟩⟨Φ𝒒|)|∂qjΦ𝒒⟩+(i↔j)=12⟨Ψ𝒒|Xi(1−|Ψ𝒒⟩⟨Ψ𝒒|)Xj|Ψ𝒒⟩+(i↔j).\displaystyle\begin{split}g_{ij}^{\mathrm{mb}}(\bm{q})&=\frac{1}{2}\left<{\partial_{q_{i}}\Phi_{\bm{q}}}\right|(1-\left|{\Phi_{\bm{q}}}\right>\left<{\Phi_{\bm{q}}}\right|)\left|{\partial_{q_{j}}\Phi_{\bm{q}}}\right>+(i\leftrightarrow j)\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left<{\Psi_{\bm{q}}}\right|X_{i}(1-\left|{\Psi_{\bm{q}}}\right>\left<{\Psi_{\bm{q}}}\right|)X_{j}\left|{\Psi_{\bm{q}}}\right>+(i\leftrightarrow j)\ .\end{split} (111)

At 𝒒=0\bm{q}=0 which means the periodic boundary condition, we then have

gi​jmb(𝟎)=12⟨Ψ𝟎|XiXj|Ψ𝟎⟩−12⟨Xi⟩⟨Xj⟩+(i↔j)=12⟨Ψ𝟎|(Xi−⟨Xi⟩)(Xj−⟨Xj⟩)|Ψ𝟎⟩+(i↔j).g_{ij}^{\mathrm{mb}}(\bm{0})=\frac{1}{2}\left<{\Psi_{\bm{0}}}\right|X_{i}X_{j}\left|{\Psi_{\bm{0}}}\right>-\frac{1}{2}\langle X_{i}\rangle\langle X_{j}\rangle+(i\leftrightarrow j)=\frac{1}{2}\left<{\Psi_{\bm{0}}}\right|(X_{i}-\langle X_{i}\rangle)(X_{j}-\langle X_{j}\rangle)\left|{\Psi_{\bm{0}}}\right>+(i\leftrightarrow j)\ . (112)

In the large size, we would have

𝒢mb=12​π​∫d2​q​gi​jmb​(𝒒)=2​π𝒱​gi​jmb​(𝟎)+O⁡(1/𝒱),\mathcal{G}^{\rm mb}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int d^{2}q\ g_{ij}^{\mathrm{mb}}(\bm{q})=\frac{2\pi}{\mathcal{V}}g_{ij}^{\mathrm{mb}}(\bm{0})+O(1/\mathcal{V})\ , (113)

which means we can use gi​jmb​(𝟎)g_{ij}^{\mathrm{mb}}(\bm{0}) to approximate 𝒢mb\mathcal{G}^{\rm mb}:

𝒢mb≈2​π𝒱gi​jmb(𝟎)=π𝒱⟨Ψ𝟎|(Xi−⟨Xi⟩)(Xj−⟨Xj⟩)|Ψ𝟎⟩+(i↔j).\mathcal{G}^{\rm mb}\approx\frac{2\pi}{\mathcal{V}}g_{ij}^{\mathrm{mb}}(\bm{0})=\frac{\pi}{\mathcal{V}}\left<{\Psi_{\bm{0}}}\right|(X_{i}-\langle X_{i}\rangle)(X_{j}-\langle X_{j}\rangle)\left|{\Psi_{\bm{0}}}\right>+(i\leftrightarrow j)\ . (114)

On the other hand, let’s look at

S(𝒒)=⟨Ψ𝟎|ρ𝒒ρ−𝒒|Ψ𝟎⟩−⟨Ψ𝟎|ρ𝒒|Ψ𝟎⟩⟨Ψ𝟎|ρ−𝒒|Ψ𝟎⟩S(\bm{q})=\left<{\Psi_{\bm{0}}}\right|\rho_{\bm{q}}\rho_{-\bm{q}}\left|{\Psi_{\bm{0}}}\right>-\left<{\Psi_{\bm{0}}}\right|\rho_{\bm{q}}\left|{\Psi_{\bm{0}}}\right>\left<{\Psi_{\bm{0}}}\right|\rho_{-\bm{q}}\left|{\Psi_{\bm{0}}}\right> (115)

with

ρ𝒒=∑𝒌,𝑸c~K,𝒌+𝒒,𝑸†​c~K,𝒌,𝑸.\rho_{\bm{q}}=\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{Q}}\tilde{c}^{\dagger}_{\text{K},\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{Q}}\tilde{c}_{\text{K},\bm{k},\bm{Q}}\ . (116)

ρ𝒒=∫d2re−i𝒒⋅𝒓n^(𝒓),n^(𝒓)=∑lc~K,l,𝒓†c~K,l,𝒓.\rho_{\bm{q}}=\int d^{2}r\,e^{-\mathrm{i}\bm{q}\cdot\bm{r}}\hat{n}(\bm{r}),\qquad\hat{n}(\bm{r})=\sum_{l}\tilde{c}^{\dagger}_{\text{K},l,\bm{r}}\tilde{c}_{\text{K},l,\bm{r}}. (117)

After subtracting the disconnected part, the N2N^{2} and Xi​jX_{ij} terms cancel, giving

S𝒒=∑i​jqi​qj​(⟨Xi​Xj⟩−⟨Xi⟩​⟨Xj⟩)+O⁡(q3).S_{\bm{q}}=\sum_{ij}q_{i}q_{j}\left(\langle X_{i}X_{j}\rangle-\langle X_{i}\rangle\langle X_{j}\rangle\right)+O(q^{3}). (120)

Therefore,

gi​jmb​(𝟎)=12​∂2S𝒒∂qi​∂qj|𝒒=𝟎,g_{ij}^{\rm mb}(\bm{0})=\frac{1}{2}\left.\frac{\partial^{2}S_{\bm{q}}}{\partial q_{i}\partial q_{j}}\right|_{\bm{q}=\bm{0}}\ , (121)

which means

𝒢mb≈2​π𝒱​gi​jmb​(𝟎)=π𝒱​∂2S𝒒∂qi​∂qj|𝒒=𝟎.\mathcal{G}^{\rm mb}\approx\frac{2\pi}{\mathcal{V}}g_{ij}^{\mathrm{mb}}(\bm{0})=\frac{\pi}{\mathcal{V}}\left.\frac{\partial^{2}S_{\bm{q}}}{\partial q_{i}\partial q_{j}}\right|_{\bm{q}=\bm{0}}\ . (122)

Owing to the momentum definite ground state that we focus on, we have

S⁡(𝒒)=⟨Ψ𝟎|ρ𝒒ρ−𝒒|Ψ𝟎⟩−δ𝒒,0N2=∑𝒌,𝒌′∑𝑸​𝑸′⟨c~†K,𝒌+𝒒,𝑸c~K,𝒌,𝑸c~†K,𝒌′,𝑸′c~K,𝒌′+𝒒,𝑸′⟩−δ𝒒,0N2=−∑𝒌,𝒌′∑𝑸​𝑸′⟨c~†K,𝒌+𝒒,𝑸c~†K,𝒌′,𝑸′c~K,𝒌,𝑸c~K,𝒌′+𝒒,𝑸′⟩+N−δ𝒒,0N2=−∑𝒌,𝒌′∑𝑸​𝑸′⟨c†𝒌+𝒒U𝑸∗(𝒌+𝒒)c†𝒌′U𝑸′∗(𝒌′)c𝒌U𝑸(𝒌)c𝒌′+𝒒U𝑸′(𝒌′+𝒒)⟩+N−δ𝒒,0N2=−∑𝒌,𝒌′M𝒌,𝒒M𝒌′,𝒒∗⟨c†𝒌+𝒒c†𝒌′c𝒌c𝒌′+𝒒⟩+N−δ𝒒,0N2=∑𝒌,𝒌′M𝒌,𝒒​M𝒌′,𝒒∗​⟨c𝒌+𝒒†​c𝒌​c𝒌′†​c𝒌′+𝒒⟩−∑𝒌M𝒌,𝒒​M𝒌,𝒒∗​⟨c𝒌+𝒒†​c𝒌+𝒒⟩+N−δ𝒒,0​N2=∑𝒌,𝒌′M𝒌,𝒒​M𝒌′,𝒒∗​⟨c𝒌+𝒒†​c𝒌​c𝒌′†​c𝒌′+𝒒⟩−∑𝒌M𝒌,𝒒​M𝒌,𝒒∗​⟨c𝒌+𝒒†​c𝒌+𝒒⟩+N−δ𝒒,0​N2.\displaystyle\begin{split}S(\bm{q})&=\left<{\Psi_{\bm{0}}}\right|\rho_{\bm{q}}\rho_{-\bm{q}}\left|{\Psi_{\bm{0}}}\right>-\delta_{\bm{q},0}N^{2}=\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\sum_{\bm{Q}\bm{Q}^{\prime}}\langle\tilde{c}^{\dagger}_{\text{K},\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{Q}}\tilde{c}_{\text{K},\bm{k},\bm{Q}}\tilde{c}^{\dagger}_{\text{K},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{Q}^{\prime}}\tilde{c}_{\text{K},\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{q},\bm{Q}^{\prime}}\rangle-\delta_{\bm{q},0}N^{2}\\ (124)

F.4 Training Data and Testing Data

In this section, we first discuss how we obtain our training and testing data, and explain the preprocessing necessary for the use of the training data in our NN.

We obtain the training and testing data via ED on the projected Hamiltonian Eq. 96 for 2×62\times 6, 3×43\times 4, 3×53\times 5, 3×63\times 6, 4×64\times 6, 5×65\times 6, 6×66\times 6 conventional meshes and a 6×26\times 2 tilted mesh, all with −2/3-2/3 electron filling (i.e., 1/31/3 hole filling). The ED spectra are summarized in Fig. 12, and the ground-state energies are listed in Tab. 10. Note that the ground state does not always have zero many-body momentum. From the ED ground state, we can then calculate the D~true\tilde{D}^{\rm true}, Q~true\tilde{Q}^{\rm true} and G~true\tilde{G}^{\rm true}, with which we can perform the interpolation training and the testing of the predictions. Specifically, for the interpolation tasks, we use 2×62\times 6, 3×43\times 4, 3×63\times 6, and tilted 6×26\times 2 for the training and 6×66\times 6 for the testing. For the interpolation training, the training data is composed of 2-RDMs over 4 different 𝒌\bm{k} point meshes: conventional 2×62\times 6, tilted 6×26\times 2, and conventional 3×43\times 4 meshes, each containing 12 𝒌\bm{k}-points, and a conventional 3×63\times 6 mesh with 18 𝒌\bm{k}-points. The tilted 6×26\times 2 mesh has M=(1101)M=\left(\begin{matrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{matrix}\right) in Eq. 20. All meshes are used for testing in the variational optimization.

For the interpolation training, we first examine the eigenvalues of D~2\prescript{2}{}{\tilde{D}} on the conventional 3×63\times 6 mesh. As shown in Fig. 13, there are no clear principal components, unlike the case for the Richardson model. Therefore, in this case, we do not use eigendecomposition for the NNs.

F.5 Framework of the NN

In this section, we discuss the framework for the NN, which is shared by both the interpolation and variational optimization. An architecture plot of the framework can be seen in Fig. 1, and we expand and generalize that description. Generally, the framework is given a momentum mesh. It then uses a NN to predict the value of an object (i.e. A𝒒A_{\bm{q}}) on that momentum mesh by evaluating the NN at each individual 𝒌\bm{k} point and aggregating the results. With this predicted object, the framework may enforce constraints (i.e. antisymmetry, PSD, particle number) by modifying the object before giving the final predicted 2-RDM object.

To use this framework, we must only provide a few key pieces of information: L1L_{1} and L2L_{2}, the momentum mesh Matrix M=(M11M12M21M22)M=\begin{pmatrix}M_{11}&M_{12}\\ M_{21}&M_{22}\end{pmatrix}) defined in (App. A), and the electron filling ν\nu. From this, the framework is able to predict the 2-RDM over this mesh. The NN framework first generates the momentum mesh; in our case, the mesh is the set (𝒌,𝒑,𝒒)(\bm{k},\bm{p},\bm{q}) where each element is over L1×L2L_{1}\times L_{2}. We map each 𝒌\bm{k} in Eq. 20 to [−1,1]2[-1,1]^{2} via

v⁡(𝒌)≡(2​(𝒂M,1⋅𝒌​mod​2​π)2​π−1,2​(𝒂M,2⋅𝒌​mod​2​π)2​π−1)=2​(k1​M11L1+k2​M21L2​mod​ 1,k1​M12L1+k2​M22L2​mod​ 1)−1,\displaystyle v(\bm{k})\equiv\left(2\frac{(\bm{a}_{M,1}\cdot\bm{k}\ \mathrm{mod}2\pi)}{2\pi}-1,2\frac{(\bm{a}_{M,2}\cdot\bm{k}\ \mathrm{mod}2\pi)}{2\pi}-1\right)=2\left(\frac{k_{1}M_{11}}{L_{1}}+\frac{k_{2}M_{21}}{L_{2}}\mathrm{mod}\,1,\frac{k_{1}M_{12}}{L_{1}}+\frac{k_{2}M_{22}}{L_{2}}\mathrm{mod}\,1\right)-1\ , (125)

with 𝒂M,1\bm{a}_{M,1} and 𝒂M,2\bm{a}_{M,2} the primitive lattice vectors. We then define the coordinate input as

𝒙v=(v⁡(𝒌),v⁡(𝒑),v⁡(𝒒))∈[−1,1]6.\bm{x}_{v}=\bigl(v(\bm{k}),\,v(\bm{p}),\,v(\bm{q})\bigr)\in[-1,1]^{6}. (126)

and the scale input as 𝒔=(1L1,1L2)\bm{s}=\left(\frac{1}{L_{1}},\frac{1}{L_{2}}\right). This 𝒔\bm{s} carries the information of the mesh, and can contain an arbitrary size amount of information about the mesh we predict on. The only requirement that the input is the same for the entire mesh, it only differs when we use the framework on different meshes. The full NN input is formed by appending 𝒔\bm{s} to 𝒙v\bm{x}_{v}, with

𝒙=(v(𝒌),v(𝒑),v(𝒒),1L1,1L2,1N)∈[−1,1]6×(0,1]3,\bm{x}=\left(v(\bm{k}),\,v(\bm{p}),\,v(\bm{q}),\frac{1}{L_{1}},\frac{1}{L_{2}},\frac{1}{N}\right)\in[-1,1]^{6}\times(0,1]^{3}, (127)

so that the final NN is a mapping Φ:ℝ9→ℝ2\Phi:\mathbb{R}^{9}\to\mathbb{R}^{2}:

Φ⁡(𝒙)=(Re([A𝒒]𝒌​𝒑),Im([A𝒒]𝒌​𝒑)).\Phi(\bm{x})=(\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}\left([A_{\bm{q}}]_{\bm{k}\bm{p}}\right),\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}\left([A_{\bm{q}}]_{\bm{k}\bm{p}}\right))\ . (128)

F.6 Interpolation Training

We first describe the interpolation training. This method is characterized by exact 2-RDM on small 𝒌\bm{k} meshes, which we use to train the NN and predict a large mesh which. For this study, we use take two choices of sampling: a single-mesh interpolation with conventional 3×63\times 6 training mesh, or a three-mesh interpolation with three training meshes (conventional 2×62\times 6, conventional 3×43\times 4, and tilted 6×26\times 2) each of which has 12 𝒌\bm{k} points. Due to the nature of ED, these smaller meshes are computationally faster to calculate, and let us investigate if this form of training can lead to more desirable results.

For the interpolation, we build a loss function with losses defined in Sec. D.1. Specifically, we use the reconstruction loss between D2\prescript{2}{}{D}, Q2\prescript{2}{}{Q}, and G2\prescript{2}{}{G} with Eq. 72, the PSD of Q2\prescript{2}{}{Q} and G2\prescript{2}{}{G} with Eq. 77 and energy distance losses with Eq. 78. For each loss, we associate a weight αi\alpha_{i} which determines its impact on training, giving us

ℒ⁡(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta) =ℒr​e​c​o​n​(θ)+αP​S​DQ​ℒP​S​DQ​(θ)+αP​S​DG​ℒP​S​DG​(θ)+αEd​i​s​t​ℒEd​i​s​t​(θ)\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{{recon}}(\theta)+\alpha_{{PSD}_{Q}}\mathcal{L}_{{PSD}_{Q}}(\theta)+\alpha_{{PSD}_{G}}\mathcal{L}_{{PSD}_{G}}(\theta)+\alpha_{E_{{dist}}}\mathcal{L}_{E_{{dist}}}(\theta) (129)

where θ\theta represents our NN’s current parameters. Additionally, the PSD loss on Q2{}^{2}Q and G2{}^{2}G is taken with respect to all meshes we train on (i.e., on which we have the ground truth), as well as the auxiliary mesh—conventional 6×66\times 6.

We run the training for Ne​p​o​c​h​s=1500N_{epochs}=1500 and train the NN using the Adam optimizer [212] with a cosine annealed [213] learning rate from η\eta to η/100\eta/100. We set Nw=800N_{w}=800 warmup epochs training the MSE loss alone (i.e. αP​S​DQ/G=αT​1=αEd​i​s​t=0\alpha_{PSD_{Q/G}}=\alpha_{T1}=\alpha_{E_{dist}}=0) so that the model does not get stuck in a non-optimal local minimum based on the other losses. Following that, we spend the next Nr=r⋅(Ne​p​o​c​h​s−Nw)N_{r}=r\cdot(N_{epochs}-N_{w}) epochs gradually increasing the penalty weights to their full reported values, where r=0.7r=0.7 is the ramping ratio. This ramp-up phase allows the model to adapt to the new penalties. Specifically, we multiply each penalty loss except the MSE by a ramp factor

ρ=min⁡(1,Nc​u​r​r​e​n​t−Nwr⁡(Ne​p​o​c​h​s−Nw)).\rho=\min\left(1,\frac{N_{current}-N_{w}}{r(N_{epochs}-N_{w})}\right). (130)

where Nc​u​r​r​e​n​tN_{current} refers to the current epoch we are training on. Once training has completed, we evaluate the NN which has the lowest loss (excluding those NNs evaluated in the warm-up and ramp phases) on the test set. The full set of hyperparameters can be seen in Tab. 11, where we provide the weights used in the loss.

As we have defined a method to interpolate from small-size 𝒌\bm{k} meshes to larger ones, we wish to benchmark the method. Specifically, we examine three factors: the impact of physics guided constraints and losses, the impact of NN architecture, and the impact of BZ sampling. To perform this evaluation, we conduct a comprehensive grid-search over every combination of NN architecture and their respective hyperparameters defined in App. C, the training on a single 3×63\times 6 mesh or three 12-𝒌\bm{k} meshes, and value of αP​S​DQ\alpha_{PSD_{Q}}, αP​S​DG\alpha_{PSD_{G}} and αEd​i​s​t\alpha_{E_{dist}}.

We first, however, examine how a Fourier interpolation performs on this data. To do so, we perform the same method as in Sec. E.3.2, calculating the FFT on the 3×63\times 6 mesh and comparing to the 6×66\times 6 mesh. With this interpolation, we find a normalized overlap of 0.648250.64825 and an R-value of 0.810490.81049, giving us a baseline for our examination.

F.6.1 Effect of Constraints and Losses

We examine the contribution of each physical constraint and loss by providing the best RvalueR_{\text{value}}, and corresponding RoverlapR_{\text{overlap}} and predicted energy on the 6×66\times 6 mesh, for predictions with the constraint or loss enabled or disabled. The training is comprehensive, and includes all 6 NNs and the training on one 3×63\times 6 or three 12−𝒌12-\bm{k} meshes. These results are given in Tab. 12. We find that while the αP​S​DQ=1\alpha_{PSD_{Q}}=1 and αP​S​DG=1\alpha_{PSD_{G}}=1 can be helpful, αEd​i​s​t=1\alpha_{E_{dist}}=1 is detrimental. Therefore, we will always keep αEd​i​s​t=0\alpha_{E_{dist}}=0. The values of αP​S​DQ\alpha_{PSD_{Q}} and αP​S​DG\alpha_{PSD_{G}} depends on the architecture as shown in the following.

We first note the Δ​Rvalue=+0.0200\Delta R_{\text{value}}=+0.0200 (the difference between on and off the constraint) for the D2{}^{2}D PSD constraint is the same as the D2{}^{2}D antisymmetry constraint and the Q​GQG reconstruction loss. This indicates that these three features together enable the best possible performance, while all three disabled account for the worst performance. Additionally, we note this performance difference is significant, as Δ​Roverlap=+0.1482\Delta R_{\text{overlap}}=+0.1482 and Δ​Ep​r​e​d=−102.918\Delta E_{pred}=-102.918. Hence, we use these three constraint and losses for further tests. For the other losses tested, we see that only PSD on Q2{}^{2}Q and G2{}^{2}G both lead to small improvements with Δ​Rvalue=+0.0016\Delta R_{\text{value}}=+0.0016 and Δ​Roverlap=0.0001\Delta R_{\text{overlap}}=0.0001 for Q2{}^{2}Q and Δ​Rvalue=0.0021\Delta R_{\text{value}}=0.0021 and Δ​Roverlap=0.0032\Delta R_{\text{overlap}}=0.0032 for G2{}^{2}G. Finally, we see that the energy distance loss had a highly negative effect, with a Δ​Rvalue=−0.0260\Delta R_{\text{value}}=-0.0260 and Δ​Roverlap=−0.1833\Delta R_{\text{overlap}}=-0.1833.

F.6.2 Architecture Comparison

For our grid search, we also examine each of our NN architectures and their hyperparameters, as defined in App. C. The result for the NN’s optimal performance are given in Tab. 13. From this, we see that the MLP has the best performance, with an R-value of 0.98230.9823 and normalized overlap of 0.97370.9737. We note that this is for a relatively large NN with 1,318,9141,318,914 parameters, while the KAN and TBN also benefit from having a larger number of parameters. The NNs that are designed explicitly for INR, SIREN and FINER, have their performance maximize at a smaller 331,778 and 134,402 parameters respectively, while the residual MLP has a similar peak at 334,210334,210 parameters.

We note that, while the MLP has the best performance, both the SIREN and Residual MLP can reach similar levels of success with RvalueR_{\text{value}} only 0.00120.0012 and 0.00050.0005 less than that of the Residual MLP. respectively. The FINER and TBN perform marginally worse, while the KAN performs the most poorly, with a peak RvalueR_{\text{value}} 0.01070.0107 less than the Residual MLP and a peak RoverlapR_{\text{overlap}} 0.05590.0559 less.

Finally, we examine the parameter efficiency plots in Fig. 14. We see that the SIREN, FINER, TBN, and residual MLP are able to achieve most of their performance with less than 10410^{4} parameters, while the MLP and KAN need far more parameters to reach their highest level of performance.

F.6.3 Mesh Comparison

We compare the single-mesh (3×6)(3\times 6) and three-mesh (3×43\times 4, 2×62\times 6, tilted 6×26\times 2) training in Tab. 14. From this result, we can see that both methods yield similar results, with marginal improvements from a three-mesh training for the SIREN with a best R-value of 0.98050.9805 vs. 0.98110.9811. The MLP, Residual MLP, KAN, FINER and TBN, on the other hand, all have a slight decrease between the two. This similarity suggests that the coverage of the 3×63\times 6 mesh is similar to that of varied meshes over different grid shapes for the purpose of interpolation training and, as smaller meshes are computationally less expensive, could provide efficiency gains for the full training process.

Overall, we select residual MLP as the model with best performance, taking into account both accuracy and energy.

F.7 Variational Optimization

In this section, we develop a method to variationally optimize our NN. Specifically, we note that the energies predicted by the interpolation-trained NNs (Sec. F.6) are far higher than the ED ground state on 6×66\times 6, and hence wish to improve the accuracy of their prediction.

To do so, we first initialize our NN pipeline with weights given by doing a 44-mesh interpolation training. Specifically, we run our NNs for Ne​p​o​c​h​s=5000N_{epochs}=5000 epochs, with a cosine scheduled learning rate from η=10−3\eta=10^{-3} to η/100\eta/100. Additionally, we use a warmup fraction of Nw=500N_{w}=500 and ramp r=0.7r=0.7. During this process, we use the reconstruction loss on 4 meshes (conventional 2×62\times 6, 3×43\times 4, 3×63\times 6, and tilted 6×26\times 2), choose αPSDQ=αPSDG=1\alpha_{\text{PSD}_{Q}}=\alpha_{\text{PSD}_{G}}=1 on the 4 meshes and an auxiliary mesh 6×66\times 6, and set αEdist=0\alpha_{E_{\text{dist}}}=0.

After the interpolation training, the NN is initialized. With an initialized NN, we then perform our variational optimization. This method works on the basis that, as our NN can make predictions an arbitrary 𝒌\bm{k} mesh, we may train the NN to make accurate predictions on a set of meshes by variationally decreasing energy over each mesh while also enforcing the Q2{}^{2}Q and G2{}^{2}G positivity conditions through ℒPSDQ/G\mathcal{L}_{\text{PSD}_{Q/G}}. The benefit of this method is two-fold: it forces the NN to care about more 22-RDMs when making predictions, and it provides an early stopping mechanism.

We first define a loss function using the PSD loss of Q2\prescript{2}{}{Q} and G2\prescript{2}{}{G}, ℒP​S​DQ/G\mathcal{L}_{PSD_{Q/G}} from Eq. 77, and the energy loss minimization loss, ℒEm​i​n\mathcal{L}_{E_{min}} from Eq. 79. The energy minimization loss is normalized per site as energy scales with NN. Hence, the full loss function is given by

ℒ⁡(θ)=αP​S​DQ​ℒP​S​DQ​(θ)+αP​S​DG​ℒP​S​DG​(θ)+∑iαEm​i​ni​ℒEm​i​ni​(θ)Nsi\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\alpha_{PSD_{Q}}\mathcal{L}_{PSD_{Q}}(\theta)+\alpha_{PSD_{G}}\mathcal{L}_{PSD_{G}}(\theta)+\sum_{i}\alpha_{E_{min}}^{i}\frac{\mathcal{L}^{i}_{{E}_{min}}(\theta)}{N_{s}^{i}} (131)

where we sum over each mesh in our energy minimization set. We note that ℒP​S​DQ\mathcal{L}_{PSD_{Q}} and ℒP​S​DG\mathcal{L}_{PSD_{G}} are evaluated on all optimization target meshes and auxiliary meshes, while ℒEm​i​ni\mathcal{L}^{i}_{{E}_{min}} only involves the optimization target meshes. Specifically, ℒEm​i​ni\mathcal{L}^{i}_{E_{min}} refers to the loss on the i​t​hith target mesh, and NsiN_{s}^{i} refers to the number of sites in that mesh. For each target mesh, we may choose an αEm​i​ni\alpha_{E_{min}}^{i} to weight the loss. Optimizing the energy on smaller target meshes is easier than on larger targe tmeshes, so we define a weight on the target meshes which scales linearly with the number of sites to encourage a more uniform convergence. Specifically, we take

αEm​i​ni=1+Nsi−1224​(κ−1)\alpha_{E_{min}}^{i}=1+\frac{N_{s}^{i}-12}{24}(\kappa-1) (132)

and we examine the impact of different κ\kappa in training. The benefit of this equation is that our smallest target meshes, with 12 𝒌\bm{k} points have, have a weight of 11, while further weights linearly increase and the weight on our 6×66\times 6 mesh is κ\kappa. We take αP​S​DQ=αP​S​DG=106\alpha_{PSD_{Q}}=\alpha_{PSD_{G}}=10^{6}.

We now establish an early stopping mechanism. Because our NN predicts and minimizes 2-RDMs over multiple mesh sizes, we may consider the energy predictions on sets of meshes the NN does not minimize energy on. This provides us a mechanism to stop training: when some validation set begins to increase it’s predicted energy dramatically, we have entered the overfitting regime. In order to implement this method, we choose a validation set of meshes and use the prediction of energy as the validation loss.

For this work, the optimization target meshes are chosen to be 3×43\times 4, 3×53\times 5, 3×63\times 6, 4×64\times 6, 5×65\times 6 and 6×66\times 6 meshes, and we optionally also include a tilted 12×412\times 4 mesh with M=(1101)M=\left(\begin{matrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{matrix}\right) in Eq. 20. For both the auxiliary meshes, we choose 2×62\times 6 and tilted 6×26\times 2, and we use the energy prediction on 2×62\times 6 as the validation loss.

To examine the effectiveness of our method, we optimize our interpolation-initialized NNs for 100,000100,000 epochs. For the first 60,00060,000 epochs, we cosine anneal the learning rate from 10−510^{-5} to 10−710^{-7}. Additionally, for this set of epochs, we using a ramp ratio r=0.05r=0.05, leading to a gradual increase in loss over 3,0003,000 epochs as defined in Eq. 130. For the next 40,00040,000 epochs, we continue to perform the minimization with a learning rate of 10−710^{-7}. We perform early stopping when the validation loss (predicted energy on the conventional 2×62\times 6 mesh) reaches 22 meV above its minimum, where the minimum is taken after the initial ramp phase to prevent any minima spikes.

We perform this examination over two seeds for randomization and take κ∈{1.5,2.0,2.5,3.0}\kappa\in\{1.5,2.0,2.5,3.0\}, and use the early stopping criteria above. We provide the results of the prediction on a 6×66\times 6 mesh with and without the tilted 12×412\times 4 mesh being the target mesh included in Tab. 15. As can be seen from these results, our variational optimization continually outperforms the pure interpolation, leading to energies that are closer to the ED ground truth while also increasing the RvalueR_{\text{value}} and RoverlapR_{\text{overlap}} scores. Our peak performance occurs for in the seed 12 trial with a κ=3.0\kappa=3.0 and no 12×412\times 4 mesh interpolation. In this trial, our NN achieved an Rvalue=0.98964R_{\text{value}}=0.98964 and Roverlap=0.98935R_{\text{overlap}}=0.98935 when evaluated on the 6×66\times 6 mesh. Additionally, its prediction on this mesh is only 0.11390.1139 meV below the ED ground state. To get a full picture of this network, we evaluate its predictions on other meshes and show them in Tab. 16.

F.8 Boundary-Point Semidefinite Programming

To compare with the neural network results, we also perform the BPSDP. We first briefly review the BPSDP algorithm described in Ref. [95]. The general algorithm is a first-order primal–dual method for solving SDP problems of the form

ESDP=minxcTx, subject to Ax=b and Mℓ(x)⪰0∀l,E_{\mathrm{SDP}}=\min_{x}\ c^{T}x,\text{ subject to }Ax=b\text{ and }M_{\ell}(x)\succeq 0\quad\forall l, (133)

where xx denotes the independent variables of the reduced density matrices, cc is the energy vector, A​x=bAx=b represents the linear equality constraints, and Mℓ​(x)M_{\ell}(x) are the matrix blocks constrained to be positive semidefinite with ll ranging over different kinds. The corresponding dual problem is

maxy,z⁡bT​y, subject to ​c−AT​y−z=0​ and ​Mℓ​(z)⪰0,\max_{y,z}\ b^{T}y,\text{ subject to }c-A^{T}y-z=0\text{ and }M_{\ell}(z)\succeq 0, (134)

where yy are called the dual variables which are also real, yy has the same length as bb, and zz is a real vector of the size xx. The BPSDP algorithm starts with an initial xx, yy and zz, and iteratively updates them until the primal error ‖A​x−b‖\|Ax-b\|, dual error ‖c−AT​y−z‖\|c-A^{T}y-z\|, and primal–dual energy difference

σ⁡(E)=|cT​x−bT​y|\sigma(E)=\left|c^{T}x-b^{T}y\right| (135)

are sufficiently small.

We adapted the algorithm proposed in Ref. [95] by incorporating the translational invariance. To be concrete, let us consider our case with only (2,2)(2,2) condition. Due to translationally invariant, xx represents all the independent real parameters in D~\tilde{D}, Q~\tilde{Q} and G~\tilde{G} tensors, and thus we can choose M1​(x)=D~M_{1}(x)=\tilde{D}, M2​(x)=Q~M_{2}(x)=\tilde{Q} and M3​(x)=G~M_{3}(x)=\tilde{G}, as all of them need to be PSD. Here the independence should also incorporates the fermionic antisymmetry in DD and QQ. The translational invariance also allows us to enforce the PSD constraints as the PSD constraints on D~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒\tilde{D}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}, Q~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒\tilde{Q}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}} and G~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒\tilde{G}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}} at each fixed 𝒒\bm{q}. cc is defined by ϵ𝒌\epsilon_{\bm{k}} and V𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒V_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}} in Eq. 96 such that

1N−1​∑𝒌,𝒒ϵ𝒌​D~𝒌,𝒌,𝒒​(x)+∑𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒V𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒​D~𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒=cT​x\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{q}}\epsilon_{\bm{k}}\tilde{D}_{\bm{k},\bm{k},\bm{q}}(x)+\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}V_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}\tilde{D}_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}=c^{T}x (136)

for any xx. Then the real matrix AA and real vector bb are defined such that A​x=bAx=b reproduces all components in Eqs. 28 and 29. The length of bb equals to the number of constraints. The translationally invariance can also be implemented for the T​1T1 and T​2T2 conditions similarly.

We first perform the BPSDP with the full (2,2)(2,2) conditions on the conventional 3×43\times 4, 3×53\times 5, 3×63\times 6, 4×64\times 6, 5×65\times 6 and 6×66\times 6, and summarize the results in Tab. 17. We note that the constraint here takes into account of all elements in Eqs. 28 and 29. The improvement after adding T​1T1 is shown in Tab. 18, where the independent components in Eq. 40 are included in A​x−bAx-b. We further add the ordinary T​2T2 condition in Tab. 19, which adds the independent components in Eq. 42 into A​x−bAx-b.
